City Guide

Berlin

Creative, raw and endlessly layered, Berlin rewards curiosity with world-class museums, waterside beer gardens, bold food, and a history that still shapes every neighborhood.
Why go: culture, nightlife, history, architecture Best time: May to Sep Ideal trip: 3–5 days Updated: February 2026

Why visit Berlin

Berlin doesn’t ask you to admire it from a distance; it invites you in. One minute you’re standing before the neoclassical sweep of Museum Island, the next you’re cycling along the former Wall, ducking into a courtyard cafe in Mitte or following basslines into Kreuzberg after dark. This is a city of reinvention, where imperial facades, postwar scars and experimental energy sit side by side.

There’s no single “Berlin experience.” Some travelers come for history: the Brandenburg Gate, the Reichstag dome, Checkpoint Charlie and the deeply moving Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe. Others arrive for creativity: gallery weekends, independent cinemas, repurposed industrial spaces, contemporary dance, vinyl shops and a famously democratic nightlife scene. Most discover it’s the combination that matters.

Lonely Planet tip Berlin is bigger than first-timers expect. Base yourself near a U-Bahn or S-Bahn line, and group sights by neighborhood rather than crisscrossing the city. A museum morning in Mitte, a canal-side lunch in Kreuzberg and a sunset in Prenzlauer Berg makes for a classic day.

Start with Berlin’s most recognizable landmark, then book ahead for the glass dome of the Reichstag for sweeping city views and a look at Norman Foster’s celebrated redesign.

Best neighborhoods

Mitte

Best for first-time visitors. Berlin’s historic core packs in headline sights, polished hotels, galleries, boutique shopping and easy transit connections.

Kreuzberg

Best for nightlife and food. Diverse, energetic and proudly independent, Kreuzberg is all canal walks, late-night shawarma, bars and creative spaces.

Prenzlauer Berg

Best for cafes and relaxed streets. Think leafy squares, bakeries, playgrounds, brunch spots and beautifully restored apartment blocks.

Friedrichshain

Best for edge and after-dark energy. Street art, riverside clubs, warehouse culture and a young local scene define this part of former East Berlin.

Charlottenburg

Best for classic Berlin. Elegant boulevards, high-end shopping along Kurfürstendamm, fine dining and the baroque Charlottenburg Palace.

Neukölln

Best for trendsetting local flavor. Rooftop bars, natural wine, Turkish markets and rapidly changing streetscapes give Neukölln its restless appeal.

Eat & drink

Berlin’s food scene is far more than currywurst, though you should absolutely try one from a beloved stand. The city’s culinary identity is shaped by migration, experimentation and affordability, which means Turkish bakeries, Vietnamese canteens, natural-wine bars, fine-dining tasting menus and old-school beer halls all coexist comfortably.

  • Try: currywurst, döner kebab, käsespätzle, schnitzel, Turkish breakfast spreads and third-wave coffee.
  • Where to graze: Markthalle Neun in Kreuzberg for street food events and local producers.
  • Sweet stop: Pick up a slice of cheesecake or a plum tart at a neighborhood konditorei.
  • Beer garden mood: Seek lakeside or park-edge spots in Tiergarten and along the Spree in summer.
“Berlin is at its best when you leave room for detours: a bakery you didn’t plan on, a courtyard cafe, a sunset on a bridge, a record shop that turns into an hour.” — Lonely Planet Local Expert

When to go

Berlin is a year-round destination, but each season has its own personality. Late spring and summer bring long evenings, lakeside escapes, open-air festivals and packed terraces. September often delivers mild weather and a cultural calendar full of exhibitions and performances. Winter can be gray, but Christmas markets, museums, concert halls and cozy bars make it atmospheric rather than sleepy.

  • May–June: Pleasant temperatures, outdoor dining, parks in bloom.
  • July–August: Festival season, warm days and the best time for lakes and open-air venues.
  • September: Excellent for city walking and fewer peak-summer crowds.
  • December: Christmas markets, mulled wine and striking winter light.

Getting around

Berlin’s integrated public transport network is one of Europe’s most efficient. U-Bahn and S-Bahn lines cover central areas and beyond, while trams are especially useful in former East Berlin. A day pass is good value if you’re making several journeys, and many central neighborhoods are excellent for cycling.

  • Validate tickets where required and keep them with you for inspection.
  • Airport trains connect BER to the city center efficiently.
  • Taxis and ride-hailing are widely available, but traffic can be slow at peak times.
  • Walking is rewarding in neighborhoods like Mitte, Kreuzberg and Prenzlauer Berg.

Practical information

Emergency 112 for ambulance and fire; 110 for police
Tipping Round up or add around 5–10% in restaurants for good service
Payment Cards are increasingly accepted, but some bars, cafes and kiosks still prefer cash
Museum planning Major museums can be busiest on weekends; reserve timed entries where possible
Sunday rhythm Most shops close on Sundays, though restaurants, museums and some stations remain lively
